entry.summary: 1 minute read DJI Osmo Pocket 4P Pearl White: price and release 2:14 As promised back when the DJI Osmo Pocket 4P officially launched in July, DJI’s flagship camera is now available in Pearl White. The DJI Osmo Pocket 4P had a convoluted journey to launch, but the story is now co
entry.content:
1 minute read
DJI Osmo Pocket 4P Pearl White: price and release
2:14

As promised back when the DJI Osmo Pocket 4P officially launched in July, DJI’s flagship camera is now available in Pearl White.

The DJI Osmo Pocket 4P had a convoluted journey to launch, but the story is now complete. The white version of the company’s flagship dual-lens gimbal camera is now available, having been listed simply as “coming soon” when its black counterpart launched globally on July 30.

It’s not just white either; it’s Pearl White. “Crafted with mica-infused pearlescent pigments and multi-layer spray coating technology, the Pearl White finish reveals subtle, soft luminous shifts across different lighting conditions and viewing angles,” says the company.

Everything else stays the same: a 1-inch CMOS sensor with 17 stops of dynamic range, the latest 10-bit D-Log 2 color profile, and dual lenses spanning 20mm to 60mm optical range. Pricing is also the same as the Classic Black model, at $619. And as you can see from the picture below, some, but not all, of its matching accessories also come in the new colorway.

"Outstanding image quality"

You can read our full review of the camera here. TL;DR we like it a lot and the image quality is outstanding, but there are a few niggles when it comes to implementation. To be fair, some of those have been addressed in firmware updates since release.

We had a bit of a dig around to see if there was any data on how different colorways performed with buyers, but couldn’t find anything beyond some old Apple data in a Fortune article from 2006 that said black nano iPods outsold white nano iPods 4:3. Oh, and a PhoneArena reader poll from 2016 suggested that out of 20 smartphone colors, ~21% of nearly 2500 participants chose white as their preference, closely followed by black with ~19%. If anyone has anything more recent, do let us know.

Either way, DJI gets another bump up to the top of the news cycle and users get another option for the Pocket 4P. Unless, of course, they live in the US. Maybe DJI should release a Space Gray version to acknowledge all the gray imports…

entry.content:
1 minute read
Antigravity A1 Follow Me Bundle: what’s included
1:31

Antigravity's Follow Me Bundle uses new accessories to transform its A1 drone with Watch and Ring Remotes into an 8K 360 follow-me drone that reliably tracks subjects while capturing every angle.

Antigravity has announced a new Follow Me Bundle, which pairs its 360-degree A1 drone with new accessories to make an 8K 360 follow-me drone.

 

The new accessories are the Watch and Ring Remotes. Antigravity says the bundle improves tracking by combining visual tracking with the Watch Remote’s built-in GPS. This, says the company, provides greater consistency during fast movements and brief obstructions.

The remotes give quick access to essential flight commands and offer manual control through Drag-to-Fly, an interesting new feature where users “grab” the drone with the Ring Remote and guide it into place with hand gestures.

After landing, users can switch between subjects and add pans and reveals from a single flight thanks to the 8K 360 capture.

The bundle also includes newly developed Full-Coverage Propeller Guards, which fully enclose the A1’s propellers for those occasions where Follow Me ventures into overly complex environments.

Pricing and availability

The Follow Me Bundle is available from October 20, 2026, through the Antigravity website and Best Buy, including BestBuy.com and 266 selected Best Buy Camera Experience Stores across the United States. Pricing is $1789 up against the standard $1599, though an introductory offer lowers that to $1469 for a limited period (and the standard bundle to $1279). More info at https://www.antigravity.tech/us/drone/antigravity-a1/buy

entry.summary: 4 minute read DaVinci Resolve Studio 21 sale: $236, 20% off 2:39 Blackmagic Design is taking 20% off DaVinci Resolve Studio and its editing keyboards and color panels until November 20. Studio drops from $295 to $236, but prices rise elsewhere across 36 of the company's products.
entry.content:
4 minute read
DaVinci Resolve Studio 21 sale: $236, 20% off
2:39

Blackmagic Design is taking 20% off DaVinci Resolve Studio and its editing keyboards and color panels until November 20. Studio drops from $295 to $236, but prices rise elsewhere across 36 of the company's products.

Blackmagic Design is getting well ahead of the annual Black Friday hoopla by offering 20% off DaVinci Resolve Studio and a range of DaVinci Resolve editing keyboards and color panels until Friday, November 20.

If the timing seems slightly odd, the company says it is tying it into the AI performance gains on the latest Apple M6 and NVIDIA RTX Spark processors.

DaVinci Resolve Studio 21 is now $236 (was $295). It adds several features over and above the free edition, namely the DaVinci Neural Engine for automatic AI region tracking, stereoscopic tools, more Resolve FX filters, more Fairlight FX audio plugins, and advanced HDR grading.

The company is also applying the same discount to grading and editing control surfaces, which can add up to some substantial savings as you move up through the pricing tiers.

On the color side, the Micro Color Panel is $449 (was $559), with controls for color grading including adding windows, and connects via Bluetooth or USB-C. The Mini Panel is $1855 (was $2319), a portable panel with three high-resolution trackballs, 12 primary corrector knobs, and LCDs with menus and buttons for switching tools, adding color nodes, and HDR and secondary grading. Then there is the top of the range Advanced Panel, which falls to $27,735 from $34,665. Designed in collaboration with professional Hollywood colorists, this provides direct access to every DaVinci color correction feature and is an object of peak desire for many who work with the software.

For editing, the Speed Editor is $349 (was $435), and promises exactly what it says on the tin with a large search dial and only the keys needed for the task in hand, plus Bluetooth with battery for wireless use. The Replay Editor, designed for multi-cam editing for news cutting and live sports replay, is $445 (was $559). And the Editor Keyboard falls to $535 from $669. It is a full-sized QWERTY keyboard in a metal design, with a metal search dial with clutch plus extra edit, trim, and timecode keys, and it can be installed inset for flush mounting.

All the hardware is available while stocks last. Some might run out fairly soon, but even at a $7k discount we’d be surprised if the Advanced Panel is facing an upcoming shortage. It is lovely though...

Price rises across 36 products

Sadly, RAMageddon has come for Blackmagic's product range elsewhere. Cameras aren't affected yet, but there are widespread price increases across 36 different products as the ocmpany is forced to pass on memory price increases.

The average rise is 30%. but some products increase way more than that. The Blackmagic 2110 IP SDI to HDMI 12G is up close to 80%, rising from $515 to $925.

"Our suppliers tell us memory consumption is now running 60% higher than it was at the peak of the COVID shortages, and even at that level they can’t keep up," says Grant Petty, Blackmagic Design CEO. "They tell us that demand is running another 30% above what they can deliver. Put together, that means demand for memory is now about double what it was at the COVID peak.

"For a few years now we have been able to hold our prices down because we had already purchased the parts and could build from that parts stock, but that stock is now being replaced with parts bought at today’s higher prices. On the products that use a lot of memory the increase is more than we can absorb. That really shows up on the new SMPTE 2110 products, which use a lot more memory.

"So we need to adjust prices on the products most affected, but only by the minimum we need to.

"I am still not happy about this though. We are going to keep searching the open market for memory and other parts at better prices, and if we can find lower cost parts we will make sure to pass the savings on through special deals, as we’ve been doing recently. Hopefully we will get back to lowering prices as soon as parts prices come back down. We think they will."

For now though, these are the rises. And while the DaVinci Resolve Studio price cut is limited to November 20, 2026, there is no indication when these will be reversed.

entry.title: Apple touchscreen MacBook Pro: October 28 launch
entry.summary: 2 minute read Apple touchscreen MacBook Pro: October 28 launch 2:59 Invites dropped to a new Apple event taking place October 28, with Pro and tell widely expected to introduce the first-ever touchscreen Macs. If the rumor mill surrounding Apple's release schedule this fall is ac
entry.content:
2 minute read
Apple touchscreen MacBook Pro: October 28 launch
2:59

Invites dropped to a new Apple event taking place October 28, with Pro and tell widely expected to introduce the first-ever touchscreen Macs.

If the rumor mill surrounding Apple's release schedule this fall is accurate (and with Apple it often is), we’re in for a busy few weeks of it with almost weekly drops coming up. HomeView debuted last week, and now coming up on October 28 is a new launch event, Pro and tell.

Like the HomeView announcement, this will be a PR drop backed up by an in-person hands-on experience for press in Los Angeles. Apple is reportedly laying on business class travel and hotel rooms for this one, so is obviously hoping to make a bit of a splash.

And it has the devices to do it. After the relative distraction of the smart home stuff last week, Bloomberg’s Apple whisperer Mark Gurman says we’re heading back into more familiar Apple territory with new MacBooks. Not just any old MacBooks either, but the first touchscreen Macs. New 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models will feature OLED displays and a Dynamic Island in place of the notch.

It’s taken close to four years for us to get here; Gurman first reported touchscreen Mac work in January 2023. But for anyone who has developed annoying longitudinal smears from their finger fruitlessly swiping their laptop screen, it will still be annoying but at least you’ll now know it did something.

Initially these machines were thought to have the latest M6 chip in, but now it seems more likely that they will have existing silicon in the shape of the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips launched in March. M6 may well feature in two other likely releases: an M6-powered 14-inch MacBook Pro, an M6 iMac with no external design change. An OLED iPad mini with a relocated camera and a revamped speaker system might also feature.

Pricing and availability

Gurman says the launch is geared toward creative professionals working in video production, photo editing, and music production. They will probably need to be working near the tops of their fields too to be able to afford them, as it is reasonable to assume that OLED and touch are expected to push prices up. Guesses are that the iPad mini alone would rise about $200 from $599 to around $799. As for the MacBooks, expect that level of increase and more.

Pre-orders on all devices should open by the end of the month.

And if those price rises look steep compared to the $299 HomeView, think of them more like representing a $299 fourth-gen Apple TV. There is a decent case to be made that all the components for the HomeView having been ring-fenced several years ago before the multiple problems with Siri AI delayed the project. Last week's Apple TV price hikes are more reflective of the environment we currently find ourselves in.

entry.title: Eddie AI update: plan first, Resolve Studio panel, and more
entry.summary: 3 minute read Eddie AI update: plan first, Resolve Studio panel, and more 5:20 Eddie AI’s latest update shows a plan before any paid run and adds a Resolve Studio panel. It also imports After Effects templates. As you would expect with NAB Show New York kicking off tomorrow, Eddi
entry.content:
3 minute read
Eddie AI update: plan first, Resolve Studio panel, and more
5:20

Eddie AI’s latest update shows a plan before any paid run and adds a Resolve Studio panel. It also imports After Effects templates.

As you would expect with NAB Show New York kicking off tomorrow, Eddie AI has added a whole raft of new features to its app that make it even more productive than before.

It’s also dropped some new features in the past 24 hours aimed at the enterprise customers it is obviously looking to talk to at the Javits Center. More about those in the video below, but highlights are bring-your-own keys with Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (ChatGPT), and Google (Gemini), on-premises running, customer IP ownership, no training on customer data, and SOC 2 Type I and II audits with GDPR certification.

These all join an impressively long list of updates.

Controlling costs

With concern rising about the costs of running AI tools, the ability to plan first is going to be a real boon. Prompts that will spend credits now return a plan that lists each step and which steps cost credits. You can approve it, change a step, or drop one, and nothing runs or is charged until you approve the list. Where a step involves a choice, such as a color grade, Eddie shows options as stills from your footage.

After Effects projects and Premiere motion graphics templates can be imported, and Eddie fills in the text and renders them in your design. It asks for any font it lacks. Brand kit headline and body fonts, colors, and logo apply to every graphic, and the motion-graphic brief shows all three before rendering. Brand fonts also apply to titles, captions, and template graphics. Thirty motion-graphic templates can be filled by named slot, placed at the playhead, and shared or copied between workspaces.

In desktop releases 4.0.38 to 4.0.43, interview cuts mixing Premiere multicam picks with plain clips rebuild as switchable multicam clips pointed at your masters (update the Premiere panel and restart Premiere). Clips with no audio import normally. The Import screen shows recent projects with thumbnails and last-opened times, and starring pins a project.

DaVinci Resolve Studio

Other links into other packages include a panel for DaVinci Resolve Studio (Workspace > Workflow Integrations > Eddie AI AE) that browses bins, imports footage, timelines, and multicam clips, and sends edits back as a new timeline. It installs from Help > Install Resolve Studio Panel… with Resolve closed, and the desktop app updates it on launch while Resolve is shut. It requires Resolve Studio from Blackmagic Design’s own installer. Sign-in and editing in the panel are not included.

And a “Source clips” export (Export menu, Footage logs) produces a Final Cut Pro browser event relinked to camera originals, carrying clip names, notes, keywords, Favorite ranges, and Rejects. You can include all clips or only labeled ones, and choose FCPXML 1.13 or 1.14. It can also be requested in chat, with the price shown first. Corrections to start timecode, frame rate, or frame size now carry into A-roll and B-roll footage logs and relink to camera originals.

The timeline also now names itself after the footage in the open edit (podcast, interview, property tour). Unused lanes fold away, and any lane with content shows. Track IDs, tool vocabulary, and NLE export track names are unchanged.

Baker's dozen of pages

Thirteen single-job pages have been added. These are take out silences, take out filler words, add animated captions, translate subtitles, dub into another language, cut a podcast into clips, edit by transcript, add B-roll, add background music, resize to vertical, clean up audio, balance speaker volume, and match a reference image to a LUT. Drop a file on a page and Eddie imports it and starts the job with the brief composed from the page and its options. Your file and options persist through sign-in.

On the audio front, each clip’s audio has its own waveform row under the picture, measured once on the server from source peaks. You can trim, split, set volume, mute, drop a clip’s audio from the edit, or restore a removed pause.

One of the surprising gaps with many AI packages is the number of insights you can get into what is being worked on. With Eddie, a new workspace menu row shows hours saved, projects run, edits exported, streak, and a shareable monthly card. Team workspaces add team totals, remaining credits with projected duration at current pace, and each member’s hours saved and edits made. Nothing ranks editors or benchmarks teams, which should help allay fears of Big Brother-esque intrusion. Personal workspaces see blurred numbers.

Eddie’s update also includes a run of smaller changes. Up to 100 mid-clip silence cuts can be made in one request, with a single undo. Razor cuts are free, and a batch of sound effects is quoted once, with a repeated sound charged once. Uploaded files can be moved to another of your projects after a dry run, with an undo. Fades can run up to six seconds, at most half of each clip they touch. They are an opacity ramp in Eddie’s rendered video and are not carried into Premiere, Resolve, Final Cut Pro, or OTIO exports. Project-wide transcript exports arrive in parts.

entry.title: Maxon 2027.0: Cinema 4D scatter, ZBrush UV Editor
entry.summary: 2 minute read Maxon 2027.0: Cinema 4D scatter, ZBrush UV Editor 4:03 Maxon’s 2027.0 release updates Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Redshift, Red Giant, and Autograph. Also new: Liquid FX foam and spray, a ZBrush UV Editor, and Scene Light relighting. Maxon has released its Fall 2026 ecosyste
entry.content:
2 minute read
Maxon 2027.0: Cinema 4D scatter, ZBrush UV Editor
4:03

Maxon’s 2027.0 release updates Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Redshift, Red Giant, and Autograph. Also new: Liquid FX foam and spray, a ZBrush UV Editor, and Scene Light relighting.

Maxon has released its Fall 2026 ecosystem update, introducing the 2027.0 releases of Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Redshift, Red Giant, and Autograph, all of which are available now.

Cinema 4D 2027.0

World building is the main leap forward with Cinema 4D 2027.0, which adds a much-requested Scatter System for procedurally populating environments with vegetation, rocks, debris, crowds, and other objects. The Scatter Generator and Scatter Tag support distribution, filtering, clustering, and transform controls, and integrate with MoGraph so Fields and Effectors can shape, animate, and influence scattered objects. Liquid FX, part of the unified simulation system, adds automatically generated foam, spray, and bubbles that respond to the underlying liquid behavior. The release also improves integration with Redshift, including ACES 2.0 alignment, and adds quality-of-life upgrades.

Pic: Jonas Pilz

There’s a decent company quote to go with this too. “A few years ago, you couldn’t simulate a beer in Cinema 4D,” comments David McGavran, CEO of Maxon. “Now you can pour it, foam it, spray it and make it look almost as satisfying as the real thing. That’s the kind of progress we want artists to feel: faster workflows, fewer barriers and more of the real world available to create.”

ZBrush and Redshift

ZBrush gains a UV Editor, built on Cinema 4D technology, for creating, editing, and refining UVs inside ZBrush, with UDIM and texel density support. New Selection Sets save and recall Polygroups, masks, Polypaint, morph targets, and UV configurations. ZBrush for iPad adds Spotlight, which covers reference, projection, painting, and image-driven sculpting, plus non-destructive 3D Layers for sculpting, polypaint, and masking.

Redshift 2027.0 has a reworked memory architecture and interactivity improvements that shorten the time between changing a scene and seeing the rendered result. Cinema 4D objects, Cloners, and particle systems can be dragged into material workflows, with their properties accessible in the Node Editor. A new procedural system generates fur, fibers, textiles, and knitted materials at render time. Support for NVIDIA RTX Spark extends Redshift to power-efficient mobile devices and production environments.

Red Giant

Scene Light, an AI-powered, depth-aware relighting tool for After Effects, is the headline addition to Red Giant 2027.0. It places lights into live-action footage and CG imagery, including interactive light from muzzle flashes, explosions, and environmental sources, and supports day-for-night treatments. Lights remain art-directable within compositing. Maxon Noise for Universe brings Cinema 4D and Redshift procedural noise patterns to video and compositing, as GPU-accelerated tools for textures, animated maps, transitions, and abstract effects.

Real Lens Flares gains Custom Schmutz, which uses the artist’s own still or animated textures for lens grime, splashes, and imperfections, plus expanded Light Source Types. Chromatic Displacement comes to Autograph, and Custom UI support in Maxon Studio lets Capsules expose Red Giant controls including color wheels, curves, gradients, and text controls.

Autograph

Finally, Autograph 2027.0 supports an MCP server, switched on by the user, that bridges AI agents to Autograph’s tools. Supported AI tools can assist with tasks, answer questions about using Autograph, or automate parts of a workflow through natural language prompts, while artists continue editing and directing in the application. Autograph also gains its first direct connection with Cinema 4D: animated elements, cameras, lights, nulls, and compatible primitives can be copied and pasted from Cinema 4D into Autograph.

entry.title: TIME Best Inventions 2026: the cameras and drones
entry.summary: 2 minute read TIME Best Inventions 2026: the cameras and drones 3:43 TIME’s 300-strong 2026 Best Inventions list features cameras from Nikon, GoPro, Fujifilm, and HoverAir. The Honor Robot Phone, Asus Zenbook Duo, and iPhone Duo are in too. The Nikon RED ZR, GoPro Mission 1 Pro I
entry.content:
2 minute read
TIME Best Inventions 2026: the cameras and drones
3:43

TIME’s 300-strong 2026 Best Inventions list features cameras from Nikon, GoPro, Fujifilm, and HoverAir. The Honor Robot Phone, Asus Zenbook Duo, and iPhone Duo are in too.

The Nikon RED ZR, GoPro Mission 1 Pro ILS, Fujifilm Instax Mini Evo Cinema, and HoverAir Aqua all made TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 list, while elsewhere there were also awards for the Honor Robot Phone, Asus Zenbook Duo, and the Apple iPhone Duo.

TIME Magazine certainly knows how to hog a news cycle. It started its Person of the Year award back in 1927 (then, inevitably Man of the Year, with the first winner being aviation pioneer Charles Lindbergh), and has curated quite a stable including the TIME100 Most Influential People, Most Influential Companies, and a whole lot more.

Apart from the years when Person of the Year goes rogue and names someone truly horrendous for their negative impacts on the world, our favorite is the Best Inventions awards, which started in 2000. As with everything else in the modern listicle- and SEO-dominated publishing industry, this has expanded hugely from an initial 35 or so entries to 300. That means it’s almost less surprising to find four cameras on the list than that there aren’t more.

These are the award-winning cameras, and there is something for everyone in there, as they also extend to drones and phones. Well, almost something for everyone, as there is no award for what is probably the hottest camera category of them all, a dedicated gimbal camera. Nor can we find any record of one in recent years, which seems a bit of an oversight.

Anyway, onwards with 2026’s crop.

2026 award winners

Nikon RED ZR: “Smartphones made quality video recording accessible to almost everyone, but there’s still a chasm between the amateur clips on TikTok and the polished productions in movie theaters,” writes TIME. “Nikon’s bid to bridge that gap is the Nikon Red ZR, an ultra-lightweight, full-frame camera designed for emerging cinematographers and high-end content producers.”

GoPro Mission 1 Pro ILS: “While action cameras can shoot anywhere, they’re not known for producing movie theater-quality footage. The GoPro Mission 1 PRO ILS shatters that silver ceiling.”

Fujifilm Instax Mini Evo Cinema: “Oodles of analog charm in a digital-friendly package,” says TIME.

HoverAir Aqua: “The team had to balance weight and waterproofing as well as figure out successful take off and landing in water, which reflects light and challenges the sensors used in most consumer drones to gauge distance from the ground.”

Honor Robot Phone: “The Honor Robot Phone includes a 360-degree rotating gimbal that, upon activation, swivels the camera out from the back of the phone, where AI software helps it track and interact with subjects, or you, in selfie mode, as they move.”

Meanwhile, other award winners that are part of the regular RedShark beat include:

Asus Zenbook Duo: “The new Asus Zenbook Duo, made with top-end components like Intel’s Core Ultra Series 3 chip and a 1TB SSD, appears indistinguishable from a conventional 14-in. touchscreen laptop. But here, the keyboard is actually a Bluetooth peripheral attached by magnets. Lift them up to reveal a second, equally vivid 14-in. touchscreen.”

Apple iPhone Duo: “Apple has been exploring the [foldable] concept for years. In 2011, when many people still carried around flip phones, Ternus and five other engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, exploring what kind of batteries and circuit boards might be needed for such an idea.”

DDJR Productions DualShot Recorder: "Influencers and hobbyists alike have long lamented the fact that smartphones can’t record horizontal and vertical video at the same time—a real annoyance when you’re trying to optimize clips for multiple platforms." And man, don't we all wish we'd thought of that one. We'd probably have enough money to buy ourselves the equally award-winning Vestaboard Note (below) if we had.

Congrats to them all.

entry.summary: 2 minute read Yashica Y16 Pocket Camera: price, specs, release 3:07 Pre-orders are open for the Yashica Y16 Pocket Camera, a 12 MP compact with a Xenon flash, optical viewfinder, and eight-filter dial. Shipping starts in late November. Yashica’s latest exercise in studied retro i
entry.content:
2 minute read
Yashica Y16 Pocket Camera: price, specs, release
3:07

Pre-orders are open for the Yashica Y16 Pocket Camera, a 12 MP compact with a Xenon flash, optical viewfinder, and eight-filter dial. Shipping starts in late November.

Yashica’s latest exercise in studied retro is the Y16 Pocket Camera, a palm-sized digital camera based on the Yashica Y16 16mm film camera introduced as far back as 1959 (the “16” refers to the 16mm film format of the original).

We’ve become used to ‘70s and ‘80s nostalgia in camera design (the recent Yashica Crew is a nod to the 1980s itself), but harking back to the 1950s and a 67-year-old design is an impressive leap. It’s not full of top-end specs as a result, but this sort of thing is extremely popular with content creators at the moment who are scouting around for something low-cost and that little bit different.

As the company puts it in its PR: "Most people carry a smartphone. Far fewer carry something that makes others stop and ask, 'What is that?'."

Y16 key specs

It's very, very flat. The $119 camera has a 12 MP sensor, an F/1.8 lens with a 4.05 mm focal length, and a 4x digital zoom. Focus range is 45 cm (18 in) to infinity. The currently all-important integrated Xenon flash has three power settings, Low, Medium, and High, with a recommended shooting range of approximately 50 cm to 2 m (20 in to 6.6 ft). One neat trick that was certainly not available in the 1950s is that the optical viewfinder has an eye sensor that automatically turns off the rear 1.45" LCD when the camera is raised to the eye.

A filter dial gives access to eight filters, allowing users to quickly switch in different looks without having to dig through menus and settings.

One place where it wins out against some of the other retro-channelling pocket cameras is that it doesn’t throw out all the nice things about the digital era. So, you still get a rear LCD and a micro SD card slot and USB-C means you do not have to rely solely on an accompanying app for viewing and distributing the photos.

Those are adequate 12 MP jpegs by default in 4:3 or 16:9, though a 5 MP mode is also available if you’re looking to conserve memory. Video is MP4 at 4K 22 fps, 2.7K 30 fps, 1080p 60 fps, and 720p 60 fps/30 fps. ISO range is 100 to 6400 / Auto.

It is, of course, smaller than the 16mm original (compared above), measuring 9.1 x 4.5 x 2.9 cm (3.6 x 1.8 x 1.1 in) and weighing 93 g (3.3 oz) with the battery. Power is via a removable 800 mAh, 3.7 V lithium battery, with USB-C. It takes microSD cards from 8 GB to 256 GB, and an 8 GB card is included.

It comes in seven colorways: Baby Blue, Baby Pink, Butter Yellow, Green, Orange, Red, and Black, all with that definite 50s vibe.

Pricing and availability

Pre-order is open now at www.yashica.com, with fulfillment expected to begin in late November 2026. The suggested retail price is $119.

entry.content:
2 minute read
Sony FX5 ship date and OM System PEN delay
2:34

The Sony FX5 is now all but confirmed for mid-November. OM Digital Solutions says some Japanese PEN pre-orders will arrive in November or later.

Whisper it slightly quietly unless the gods listen and decide that we’re all tempting fate way too much, but it looks like the delayed Sony FX5 may actually meet its revised November 16 ship date.

One of the websites keeping closest tabs on the whole affair is sonyalpharumors. It reports that a small number of users who actually received their cameras in August and had to ship them back for repair now either have the repaired units back in their hands or have received a note saying that they will be on its way to them in October.

Sony’s European sites now list November 16 as the shipping date, while in the US, Adorama lists availability starting November 15 and has sent out this note.

Dear Customer
We’re pleased to share an update on the Sony FX5.
Sony has completed its final quality assurance process. Based on the latest information, customer deliveries are currently anticipated in early to mid-November.
Thank you for your patience and continued support. We look forward to getting you your FX5 to you as soon as possible.
Sincerely,
The Adorama Team.]

All this will come into focus soon and the good news for the thousands of people who seem to have placed pre-orders (it ranks as the number one release in Amazon’s Professional Grade Video Cameras listings despite being unavailable) is that the long and needlessly messy saga may be finally drawing to a close.

OM System PEN delays

Meanwhile, in its home market of Japan, the new OM System PEN has proved so popular that there is now a backlog.

“Regarding the OM SYSTEM PEN and related accessories, scheduled for release in late October 2026, we would like to inform you of the following about product deliveries in Japan,” says a company statement.

“We have received a very large number of pre-orders for this product, and some customers may not receive their orders until November or later. We deeply apologize for the great inconvenience this causes to customers who are waiting for the product and to everyone else involved.”

The camera was scheduled for a late October release. The situation may be better outside of Japan, with both US and UK sites accepting pre-orders. The US site goes as far as saying that the estimated release date is today, October 14, while the UK lists a delivery lead time of 2-3 weeks.

Unlike with the FX5 there seem to be no production issues in what may, or may not, be a global delay; just a case of demand outstripping supply according to the company. We’ll keep an eye on it all and update when we can.

entry.content:
2 minute read
Digger and VistaVision: box office flop explained
3:30

Digger opened to just $20 million worldwide on a reported $125 million-plus budget. The VistaVision-shot satire shows no format can carry a film alone.

Back in July, an interview was released with Tom Cruise talking about the use of VistaVision in his then upcoming movie satire Digger. It was notable for the fact that, whatever you may think of him personally, Cruise has a definite feel for the craft of making films. In it he talks about the different film and digital formats used in his movies over the years, shows a great understanding of lenses, and also talks about making movies look like movies.

Digger is a satirical comedy from Alejandro G. Iñárritu, starring Cruise as oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Emmanuel “Chivo” Lubezki ASC AMC is the cinematographer, reuniting with Iñárritu after Birdman and The Revenant. On paper it all works fine, but it’s currently on track to be one of the biggest flops in Hollywood history.

Estimates are that when you factor in marketing costs, Digger has to make somewhere between $300 and $350 million to break even. It opened at a meager $20 million worldwide, and Variety estimates that it is on track to lose around $245 million over its theatrical run.

This caps an awful run of movies for Warner Bros., now of course part of Skydance, which now must just be closing its corporate eyes and wishing for the release of Dune: Part 3 in December.

VistaVision’s hot run comes to an end

Cruise says the production tested VistaVision against 65mm, and in winning that screening battle, VistaVision has its first notable flop of the modern era.

The format runs 35mm film horizontally through the camera, so each frame spans eight perforations instead of the usual four, roughly doubling the negative area per frame. Paramount developed it in the 1950s, and it was used on films including White Christmas and Hitchcock’s Vertigo and North by Northwest, before the cameras then effectively sat on storeroom shelves for six decades.

The modern revival came with The Brutalist, shot mostly in VistaVision by Lol Crawley, who won the 2025 cinematography Oscar. That sort of thing gains attention and, as a cheaper alternative to shooting 65mm, even VistaVision’s use of problematic and noisy kit has failed to dampen enthusiasm for the format. Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another reportedly ran around 1.5 million feet (457 km, or 284 miles) of film through its antique cameras. Bugonia used a Wilcam W11, and Wuthering Heights and Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew have also gone the same route. M. Night Shyamalan’s Remain is reported as next.

Lubezki shot Digger in 8-perf VistaVision on a Beaumont camera, with custom-adapted Panavision lenses that include a 29mm used for much of the film. It was not the only camera. A Sony Venice 2 and an ARRI Alexa Mini LF served as B cameras.

The fact that it was shot primarily on VistaVision, though, has been used as a peg in the marketing of the film, as the Why ‘Digger’ needed to be filmed in VistaVision video below shows.

But if Digger shows anything it’s that, with the exception perhaps of native IMAX 70mm, audiences care less about what a film was shot on than whether it’s any good or not.  Have to say, it does look lovely though.
